input.prompt:
Explore this Next.js codebase to understand its structure. I need to know:
1. The Next.js config file (next.config.js, next.config.mjs, next.config.ts, etc.) and its contents
2. The app directory structure (especially layout files and page files)
3. The package.json to understand the Next.js version being used
4. Any existing experimental flags in the config

Return the full contents of the config file, package.json (just the dependencies section), and list all files in the app/ directory.

state.output:
Here is a complete overview of the Next.js codebase:

---

## 1. Next.js Config File: `/vercel/sandbox/next.config.ts`

```ts
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {}

export default nextConfig
```

The config is **empty** -- there are no experimental flags, no custom webpack config, no redirects/rewrites, nothing. It's the bare minimum setup using the TypeScript config format (`next.config.ts`).

---

## 2. App Directory Structure

All 4 files live directly under `/vercel/sandbox/app/` (no nested routes):

| File | Path | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| `layout.tsx` | `/vercel/sandbox/app/layout.tsx` | Root layout -- sets `<html lang="en">` with a `<body>` wrapper. Exports metadata (title: "Create Next App"). |
| `page.tsx` | `/vercel/sandbox/app/page.tsx` | Root page (home route `/`). Renders `<ProductList>` and `<Recommendations>` each wrapped in `<Suspense>` boundaries with fallback loading text. |
| `ProductList.tsx` | `/vercel/sandbox/app/ProductList.tsx` | Server component. Fetches products from `https://api.example.com/products` and renders a list with name/price. |
| `Recommendations.tsx` | `/vercel/sandbox/app/Recommendations.tsx` | Server component. Fetches recommendations from `https://api.example.com/recommendations` and renders a list with item names. |

Notable: Both `ProductList` and `Recommendations` are **async Server Components** that fetch data at render time. The `page.tsx` wraps each in `<Suspense>` to allow streaming/partial rendering.

---

## 3. Package.json Dependencies (from `/vercel/sandbox/package.json`)

**dependencies:**
| Package | Version |
|---|---|
| `next` | `^16.2.1-canary.45` |
| `react` | `19.1.0` |
| `react-dom` | `19.1.0` |

**devDependencies:**
| Package | Version |
|---|---|
| `@types/node` | `^20` |
| `@types/react` | `^19` |
| `@types/react-dom` | `^19` |
| `@vitejs/plugin-react` | `^4.4.1` |
| `typescript` | `^5` |
| `vite-tsconfig-paths` | `^5.1.4` |
| `vitest` | `^3.1.3` |

Key takeaway: This is running **Next.js 16 (canary)**, which is a pre-release version ahead of the stable line. The presence of `@vitejs/plugin-react`, `vite-tsconfig-paths`, and `vitest` in devDependencies suggests Vitest-based testing.

---

## 4. Experimental Flags

**There are no experimental flags in the config.** The `nextConfig` object is completely empty (`{}`). The AGENTS.md file does warn that this version may have breaking changes, so the canary tag (`^16.2.1-canary.45`) is significant.

00014| Partial Prerendering (PPR) combines static and dynamic rendering in a single route. At build time, Next.js generates a static HTML shell and a `postponedState` blob for each PPR-enabled route. At request time, the shell is served immediately and dynamic portions are rendered and streamed to the client.
00015| 
00016| This page explains how platforms can implement PPR support at different levels of sophistication.
00017| 
00018| ## How PPR Works
00019| 
00020| ### Build time
00021| 
00022| For each PPR route, Next.js produces:
00023| 
00024| - A **static HTML shell** containing all the content that can be prerendered, with [Suspense](/docs/app/guides/streaming#what-is-streaming) fallbacks where dynamic content will appear.
00025| - A **`postponedState`** value: a serialized string. Treat it as opaque: pass it through without parsing or modifying it. Altering `postponedState` produces incorrect dynamic rendering output.
00026| - An **RSC payload** for the static portions of the page.
00027| 
00028| ### Request time
00029| 
00030| When a request arrives for a PPR route:
00031| 
00032| 1. The server sends the static HTML shell to the client immediately.
00033| 2. The server resumes rendering the dynamic portions using the postponed state.
00034| 3. Dynamic content is streamed to the client, allowing React to hydrate the deferred Suspense boundaries.
00035| 
00036| The client sees the static shell instantly, then dynamic content appears as it resolves.
00037| 
00038| ## Storing PPR Artifacts
00039| 
00040| Each PPR route requires two artifacts to be stored together:
00041| 
00042| 1. The static HTML shell.
00043| 2. The `postponedState` blob.
00044| 
00045| These must be stored and updated atomically. When a PPR route is revalidated (via [time-based](/docs/app/guides/incremental-static-regeneration) or [on-demand revalidation](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/revalidateTag)), Next.js regenerates both the shell and the postponed state together. Serving a new shell with an old postponed state, or vice versa, will produce incorrect dynamic content.
00046| 
00047| Use [`requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2`](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter) in your adapter to observe cache updates and propagate them to your storage backend.
00048| 
00049| ## Origin-Only Implementation
00050| 
00051| **This is the simplest approach and works on every platform that supports streaming HTTP responses.**
00052| 
00053| All requests go directly to the Next.js server. The server reads the shell from its local cache, sends it, then renders and streams the dynamic content. This is what `next start` does by default.
00054| 
00055| No additional infrastructure is needed. If your platform supports streaming HTTP responses, it supports PPR.
00056| 
00057| ## CDN Shell + Origin Compute
00058| 
00059| For better TTFB, the static HTML shell can be cached at the CDN edge. When a request arrives:
00060| 
00061| 1. The CDN serves the cached shell immediately (edge latency).
00062| 2. The CDN sends a resume request to the origin server (ideally in parallel with streaming the shell).
00063| 3. The origin server renders only the dynamic portions and streams them back.
00064| 4. The CDN concatenates the shell and dynamic content into a single streaming response to the client.
00065| 
00066| This requires the CDN to support a mechanism for combining cached and dynamic content in a single streaming response. The static shell TTFB drops to edge latency while dynamic content still streams from origin.
00067| 
00068| For the lowest possible latency, the shell can be served from edge storage (for example, a KV store populated during `onBuildComplete`) rather than from a CDN cache. This is a platform architecture decision and does not require any changes to the Next.js application.
00069| 
00070| ## The Resume Protocol
00071| 
00072| The **resume protocol** tells the Next.js handler to skip the shell and render only the dynamic portions. It is used by CDN-to-origin architectures and adapter-based deployments that serve the shell separately.
00073| 
00074| In standard `next start`, the server handles both the shell and dynamic render in a single pass automatically.
00075| 
00076| ### CDN-to-origin
00077| 
00078| When the CDN makes an HTTP request to a separate Next.js origin:
00079| 
00080| - Send a **POST** request to the route with the header `next-resume: 1`.
00081| - Include the `postponedState` blob as the **request body**.
00082| - The server will render only the deferred Suspense boundaries and stream the result.
00083| 
00084| > **Good to know:** When a POST request combines a Server Action with a PPR resume, the request body contains the postponed state followed by the action body. The `x-next-resume-state-length` header carries the byte length of the postponed state prefix so the handler can separate the two. For a pure PPR resume (the common case), the entire request body is the postponed state and this header is not needed.
00085| 
00086| ### Adapter-based
00087| 
00088| When the platform invokes the handler function directly:
00089| 
00090| - Call the entrypoint handler with `req.method` set to `'POST'`, the `next-resume: 1` header on the request, and the `postponedState` as the request body. (You can also pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` as the third argument to the handler invocation, which is equivalent but bypasses the HTTP layer entirely.)
00091| - The handler renders only the deferred Suspense boundaries and streams the result to `res`.
00092| - No HTTP round-trip is needed: the handler is invoked in-process.
00093| 
00094| ### Finding PPR routes in build output
00095| 
00096| In the [adapter output](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/output-types), PPR routes are identified by `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'` in the prerenders array. Iterate `outputs.prerenders` to find these entries and read `fallback.postponedState`.
00097| 
00098| `pprChain.headers` contains the headers needed for the resume protocol: `{ 'next-resume': '1' }`.
00099| 
00100| For detailed implementation with code examples, see [Implementing PPR in an Adapter](/docs/app/api-reference/adapters/implementing-ppr-in-an-adapter).
00101| 
00102| ## Implementation Checklist
00103| 
00104| 1. **Read PPR outputs at build time.** In your adapter's `onBuildComplete`, identify prerenders with `renderingMode: 'PARTIALLY_STATIC'`. Store the shell HTML and `postponedState` in your cache.
00105| 
00106| 2. **Serve the shell at request time.** For incoming requests to PPR routes, serve the cached shell immediately and begin streaming.
00107| 
00108| 3. **Resume dynamic rendering.** For CDN-to-origin: send a POST request to the Next.js handler with the `next-resume: 1` header and the postponed state as the body. For adapter-based: call the handler directly with POST method and the postponed state in the request body (or pass `requestMeta: { postponed: postponedState }` to the handler). Stream the response back to the client.
00109| 
00110| 4. **Handle cache updates.** Use `requestMeta.onCacheEntryV2` to capture new shell + postponed state pairs after revalidation, and update your cache atomically.
00111| 
00112| 5. **Support graceful degradation.** If the postponed state is unavailable or stale, fall back to a full server render. The user gets a complete page without the shell-first optimization.
00113| 
00114| For the complete adapter API reference and implementation examples, see the [Deployment Adapter API](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/adapterPath).
00115| 

(End of file - total 115 lines)

00004| ---
00005| 
00006| Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive. Data fetching is dynamic by default, and you choose what to cache at the page, component, or function level. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route.
00007| 
00008| ## Usage
00009| 
00010| To enable the `cacheComponents` flag, set it to `true` in your `next.config.ts` file:
00011| 
00012| ```ts filename="next.config.ts"
00013| import type { NextConfig } from 'next'
00014| 
00015| const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
00016|   cacheComponents: true,
00017| }
00018| 
00019| export default nextConfig
00020| ```
00021| 
00022| When `cacheComponents` is enabled, you can use the following cache functions and configurations:
00023| 
00024| - The [`use cache` directive](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache)
00025| - The [`cacheLife` function](/docs/app/api-reference/config/next-config-js/cacheLife) with `use cache`
00026| - The [`cacheTag` function](/docs/app/api-reference/functions/cacheTag)
00027| 
00028| > **Good to know**: If you used `experimental.useCache` or `experimental.dynamicIO`, migrate using the [Version 16 upgrade guide](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#experimentaldynamicio-and-experimentalusecache). To migrate route segment configs and other caching patterns, see [Migrating to Cache Components](/docs/app/guides/migrating-to-cache-components).
00029| 
00030| Additionally, `cacheComponents` implements **[Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/glossary#partial-prerendering-ppr)** as the default behavior in the App Router. This means the `experimental.ppr` configuration flag and the `experimental_ppr` route segment configuration are no longer necessary and have been removed.
00031| 
00032| Read [How rendering works](/docs/app/getting-started/caching#how-rendering-works) for how the static shell and streaming fit together.
00033| 
00034| > **Good to know**: If you used experimental PPR in Next.js 15, refer to the [Partial Prerendering (PPR)](/docs/app/guides/upgrading/version-16#partial-prerendering-ppr) section of the Version 16 upgrade guide when migrating.
00035| 
00036| ## Navigation with Activity
00037| 
00038| When `cacheComponents` is enabled, Next.js uses React's [`<Activity>`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity) component to preserve component state during client-side navigation.
00039| 
00040| Rather than unmounting the previous route when you navigate away, Next.js sets the Activity mode to [`"hidden"`](https://react.dev/reference/react/Activity#activity). This means:
00041| 
00042| - Component state is preserved when navigating between routes
00043| - When you navigate back, the previous route reappears with its state intact
00044| - Effects are cleaned up when a route is hidden, and recreated when it becomes visible again
00045| 
00046| This behavior improves the navigation experience by maintaining UI state (form inputs, or expanded sections) when users navigate back and forth between routes.
00047| 
00048| > **Good to know**: Next.js uses heuristics to keep a few recently visited routes `"hidden"`, while older routes are removed from the DOM to prevent excessive growth.
00049| 
00050| Some UI patterns behave differently when components stay mounted instead of unmounting. See the [Preserving UI state guide](/docs/app/guides/preserving-ui-state) for handling common patterns like dropdowns, dialogs, and testing.
00051| 
00052| ## Version History
00053| 
00054| | Version | Change                                                                                                                            |
00055| | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
00056| | 16.0.0  | `cacheComponents` introduced. This flag controls the `ppr`, `useCache`, and `dynamicIO` flags as a single, unified configuration. |

title: cacheComponents
description: Learn how to enable the cacheComponents flag in Next.js.
---

Cache Components enables component and function-level caching using the [`use cache`](/docs/app/api-reference/directives/use-cache) directive. Data fetching is dynamic by default, and you choose what to cache at the page, component, or function level. Next.js prerenders a static HTML shell that is served immediately while dynamic content streams in when ready, letting you mix static and dynamic content within a single route.

## Usage

To enable the `cacheComponents` flag, set it to `true` in your `next.config.ts` file:

```ts filename="next.config.ts"
import type { NextConfig } from 'next'

const nextConfig: NextConfig = {
  cacheComponents: true,
}

export default nextConfig
```
